framed_question: How can the Tabler skill be improved? What's missing, weak, redundant, or could be better structured? Consider: clarity, completeness, triggering accuracy, examples, edge cases, anti-patterns, organization, and real-world effectiveness.

advisors.name: The Contrarian
advisors.response: This skill is a reference dump, not a skill. It's 15 markdown files of raw HTML snippets with almost zero decision guidance. An agent reading this still won't know WHEN to use a card vs a panel, WHEN to reach for a modal vs an offcanvas, or HOW to choose between similar patterns. The 'Component Routing' section is just a file listing — it doesn't route anything. There's no prioritization, no 'start here,' no anti-patterns section telling agents what NOT to do. The color reference in SKILL.md duplicates what's in colors-typography.md, and the size reference duplicates component-level docs. The Bootstrap integration section is a liability — it gives agents license to use any Bootstrap class without understanding Tabler's overrides, which is how you get broken UIs that look almost right. The evals test whether agents use 'real Tabler classes' but the skill itself doesn't define what 'real' means beyond showing examples. There's no versioning strategy — Tabler 2.x is on the horizon and this skill has no migration guidance or even awareness. The 'last_verified' field is theater — it says 2026-03-19 but there's no verification process documented. The skill is structurally complete but functionally shallow: it tells you what the pieces look like but never how to compose them or what can go wrong.

advisors.name: The First Principles Thinker
advisors.response: What problem does this skill actually solve? The agent needs to produce correct Tabler HTML. But 'correct' means three things: (1) valid class names that exist in the framework, (2) proper structural hierarchy so components render correctly, and (3) appropriate component choice for the UX context. This skill only addresses #1, and barely — it lists examples but doesn't define the boundaries of the class namespace. An agent can't tell if `.card-body-lg` exists or not from this skill. The fundamental architecture is wrong: a skill should be a decision tree, not an encyclopedia. The agent's real question is 'I need to show X to the user — what do I build?' not 'show me 400 lines about modals.' The skill should be structured as: (a) a component selection guide (when to use what), (b) a minimal correct template per component, (c) common composition patterns, and (d) a gotchas/anti-patterns section. Everything else — the exhaustive variant lists — should be secondary reference material that the agent only pulls when needed. The current structure front-loads reference material and buries the decision logic. The page-patterns file is the closest thing to useful, but it's buried at the bottom of the routing table. The skill should be inverted: patterns first, reference second.

advisors.name: The Expansionist
advisors.response: This skill is leaving enormous value on the table. First, it has zero integration guidance for the actual stack this repo targets — Django, HTMX, and Tabler are used together everywhere, but this skill treats Tabler as a standalone static HTML framework. There's no mention of how Tabler components work with HTMX swap targets, how Django form rendering maps to Tabler's form structure, or how to handle CSRF tokens in Tabler modals. Second, the skill has no accessibility guidance — Tabler has specific ARIA patterns, focus management requirements for modals, and screen-reader considerations that are completely absent. Third, there's no dark mode coverage — Tabler supports it natively and the skill doesn't mention it once. Fourth, the skill could include a 'Tabler class existence checker' — a definitive list of valid classes so agents can validate their output instead of guessing. Fifth, the patterns file covers 8 page types but misses critical ones: login/auth flows, error pages, onboarding wizards, notification centers, and data-heavy admin tables with filtering. Sixth, there's no mention of Tabler's JavaScript API — when to use `data-bs-toggle` vs custom JS initialization, how to programmatically open modals, how to handle toast notifications. The skill could be the definitive bridge between design and implementation for the entire stack, but right now it's just a HTML snippet library.

advisors.name: The Outsider
advisors.response: I have no context about this project. Reading SKILL.md, I can't tell: (1) what this skill is FOR — is it a reference? A tutorial? A cheat sheet? The description says 'comprehensive reference guide' but the quick start says 'identify the component you need' which implies it's a lookup tool, yet there's no lookup mechanism beyond reading file names. (2) The 'scope: tabler' and 'target_versions: Tabler 1.x' frontmatter means nothing to me — I don't know what Tabler is, and the skill doesn't explain. (3) The routing table lists 14 reference files but gives me no sense of which ones I'll actually need for a typical task. (4) The color reference section lists color names but doesn't show me what they look like or when to use semantic vs theme colors. (5) The Bootstrap integration section is confusing — is Tabler built on Bootstrap or is it a separate framework? The relationship is never explained. (6) There are no links to external documentation, no 'see also' to the official Tabler docs, no way for me to verify if the information is current. (7) The evals test whether the agent uses 'real Tabler classes' but I can't tell from the skill which classes are real vs invented. The skill assumes I already know Tabler well enough to use it, which defeats the purpose of a skill.

advisors.name: The Executor
advisors.response: The fastest improvement: restructure SKILL.md as a decision guide, not a table of contents. Current SKILL.md is ~120 lines of overview + color/size reference + Bootstrap integration. Replace it with: (1) a 10-line 'if you need X, use Y' component selection table, (2) a 'start with these 3 files' section pointing to page-patterns.md, cards.md, and form-elements.md since those cover 80% of real tasks, (3) a 15-line anti-patterns section covering the most common mistakes (wrong card nesting, missing role attributes, mixing Bootstrap JS with Tabler's API), (4) remove the duplicated color/size reference from SKILL.md — it's already in the reference files. Second: add a 'Tabler + HTMX' integration note since this repo is Django+HTMX+Tabler — even 5 lines about swap targets and modal triggers would prevent the most common integration bugs. Third: add dark mode to colors-typography.md — it's a real feature that agents will need. Fourth: add a 'valid classes' validation section or regex so agents can self-check. Fifth: fix the 'last_verified' process — either automate it or remove it. The current approach of stamping a date with no verification process is worse than no date at all because it creates false confidence. Do these five things and the skill goes from reference dump to actually useful.

peer_reviews.strongest: B (The First Principles Thinker) — correctly identifies that the skill is structured as an encyclopedia when it should be a decision tree. The 'patterns first, reference second' insight is the single most impactful structural change possible. The three-part definition of 'correct' (valid classes, proper hierarchy, appropriate choice) gives a clear framework for measuring skill quality.
peer_reviews.biggest_blind_spot: D (The Outsider) — correctly flags the missing Tabler explanation and external doc links, but underestimates the value of stack-specific integration. The suggestion to add accessibility guidance (from C) is important but D doesn't engage with it. Also, D's confusion about scope/target_versions is valid but the fix is trivial — a one-line explanation in the description would suffice.
peer_reviews.what_all_missed: None of the advisors addressed the eval alignment problem. The evals test for 'real Tabler classes' but the skill doesn't provide a validation mechanism. If the skill added a class existence reference, the evals would become meaningful instead of subjective. Also, none mentioned that the skill has no changelog or versioning strategy for its own content — when Tabler updates, how does the skill signal what changed?

peer_reviews.strongest: E (The Executor) — the five concrete steps are immediately actionable and correctly prioritized. The 'start with these 3 files' suggestion alone would dramatically improve agent performance. The anti-patterns section is the highest-ROI addition because it prevents the most common failure mode: agents producing plausible-looking but broken HTML. The call to remove or automate 'last_verified' is overdue.
peer_reviews.biggest_blind_spot: A (The Contrarian) — correctly identifies the Bootstrap integration section as a liability but doesn't propose a fix beyond implying it should be removed. The Bootstrap relationship is real and necessary — Tabler IS built on Bootstrap — so the answer isn't removal, it's clearer guidance on which Bootstrap utilities are safe to use and which conflict with Tabler's styling. A also flags the versioning concern but offers no migration strategy.
peer_reviews.what_all_missed: No advisor addressed the skill's total absence of responsive design guidance beyond 'use Bootstrap responsive classes.' Real Tabler layouts require understanding specific responsive patterns — when to use `.col-md-*` vs custom breakpoints, how card grids collapse, how tables handle overflow. This is a gap that causes real UI bugs.

peer_reviews.strongest: C (The Expansionist) — the identification of missing stack integration (Django + HTMX + Tabler) is the most valuable observation because it addresses the actual use case this repo serves. The accessibility gap is a real risk — agents building modals without proper ARIA attributes will produce inaccessible UIs. The dark mode omission is surprising given that Tabler has first-class dark mode support and agents will encounter it in real projects.
peer_reviews.biggest_blind_spot: B (The First Principles Thinker) — the 'decision tree' framing is correct in theory but B doesn't acknowledge the legitimate value of having comprehensive reference material available. The skill needs to serve both the agent who needs a quick answer AND the agent who needs deep reference. B's suggestion to make everything 'secondary reference material' risks making the skill harder to navigate for advanced users. The right answer is a two-layer structure: quick decision guide on top, comprehensive reference below.
peer_reviews.what_all_missed: None of the advisors addressed the skill's lack of a 'common mistakes' or 'troubleshooting' section. When an agent's Tabler output looks wrong, they need debugging guidance: 'if your modal isn't showing, check X; if your card layout is broken, check Y.' This would be more valuable than additional reference material.

peer_reviews.strongest: A (The Contrarian) — the observation that the skill is 'structurally complete but functionally shallow' is the most honest assessment. The critique of 'last_verified' as theater is spot-on — a date stamp without a verification process is actively misleading. The point about the evals testing 'real Tabler classes' without defining what 'real' means is a genuine quality issue that undermines the entire eval framework.
peer_reviews.biggest_blind_spot: C (The Expansionist) — while the integration suggestions are valuable, C's list of missing patterns (login flows, error pages, onboarding wizards) would bloat the skill without clear prioritization. Not every page pattern needs to be in the skill — some can be composed from existing components. C also doesn't address the maintenance burden: every addition to the skill increases the cost of keeping it current with Tabler releases.
peer_reviews.what_all_missed: No advisor discussed the skill's relationship to the official Tabler documentation. Should this skill be a standalone reference, or should it be a curated supplement that points to official docs for exhaustive detail? The current approach tries to be standalone but ends up being a partial copy of the official docs, which will inevitably drift out of date.

peer_reviews.strongest: D (The Outsider) — the observation that the skill assumes prior Tabler knowledge is the most important finding for triggering accuracy. If an agent doesn't know what Tabler is, it won't trigger this skill at all, and the skill's content won't help it decide. The suggestion to add external doc links and explain the Bootstrap relationship addresses a real discoverability problem. The confusion about whether Tabler is built on Bootstrap or separate is a genuine ambiguity that the skill should resolve in the first paragraph.
peer_reviews.biggest_blind_spot: E (The Executor) — while the five steps are actionable, they're all structural/content changes. E doesn't address the triggering problem: the skill's description says 'Tabler UI components, CSS classes, variants, or layout patterns' but an agent searching for 'card design' or 'modal dialog' or 'form styling' might not think to trigger this skill. The description could be improved with more natural-language trigger phrases.
peer_reviews.what_all_missed: None of the advisors addressed the skill's handling of Tabler's JavaScript components vs pure CSS components. The skill mixes them without clearly distinguishing which components require JS initialization and which don't. This leads to agents copying HTML for modals, dropdowns, or tooltips without including the necessary JS initialization code, producing non-functional UI.

chairman_verdict.agrees: The council unanimously agrees the skill is structurally complete but functionally shallow. All five advisors identified the core problem: the skill is organized as a reference encyclopedia when it should be a decision guide. There is strong agreement on three specific gaps: (1) no anti-patterns or common mistakes section, (2) no stack integration guidance (Django + HTMX + Tabler), (3) no accessibility coverage. Four of five advisors flagged the 'last_verified' date as misleading without a verification process. The council also agrees the Bootstrap integration section needs clarification, not removal.
chairman_verdict.clashes: The main clash is between B (First Principles) who wants to restructure everything as a decision tree with reference material as secondary, and C (Expansionist) who wants to add more content (integration guides, accessibility, dark mode, more patterns). B fears bloat; C fears gaps. The resolution is a two-layer structure: a lean decision guide on top with comprehensive reference below. A second clash: C and D want more content (explanations, external links, stack integration) while E wants to focus on the highest-ROI structural changes first. The council should do E's five steps as phase one, then address C and D's suggestions as phase two.
chairman_verdict.blind_spots: The council missed three things: (1) no discussion of the skill's relationship to official Tabler docs — should it be standalone or a curated supplement? (2) no mention of responsive design patterns beyond 'use Bootstrap classes' — this causes real UI bugs. (3) no discussion of JS vs CSS component distinction — agents need to know which components require JS initialization. Additionally, no advisor addressed triggering accuracy or the skill's description language, which Reviewer 5 identified as a real problem.
chairman_verdict.recommendation: Restructure the skill in two phases. Phase one (immediate): (1) Rewrite SKILL.md as a decision guide with component selection table, anti-patterns section, and 'start with these 3 files' onboarding. (2) Remove duplicated color/size reference from SKILL.md. (3) Add a 15-line Tabler + HTMX integration note. (4) Fix or remove 'last_verified.' (5) Add dark mode coverage to colors-typography.md. Phase two (follow-up): (1) Add accessibility guidance (ARIA patterns, focus management). (2) Add a troubleshooting/common mistakes section. (3) Clarify the JS vs CSS component distinction. (4) Add external doc links and explain Bootstrap relationship in the first paragraph. (5) Expand page patterns to include login/auth flows and error pages. Throughout, maintain the two-layer structure: decision guide on top, comprehensive reference below.
chairman_verdict.first_step: Rewrite SKILL.md as a decision guide. Replace the current ~120-line overview with: (1) a 10-line component selection table ('if you need X, use Y'), (2) a 'start here' section pointing to page-patterns.md, cards.md, and form-elements.md, (3) a 15-line anti-patterns section covering wrong card nesting, missing role attributes, and Bootstrap/Tabler conflicts, (4) remove the duplicated color/size reference. This single change addresses the unanimous council finding and can be done in under an hour.
